children: By Paul Hannon

The eurozone economy picked up more rapidly than previously estimated in the three months through June despite the jump in energy prices caused by the war between the U.S. and Iran, but that resilience will be challenged if the conflict continues to block the Strait of Hormuz.
Figures released Monday showed the surprisingly strong expansion recorded in the second quarter was driven by exports and consumer spending.

However, economists warn that higher energy bills will likely take a toll on household spending as cold weather returns, while some of the unexpected strength of overseas sales may be a short-lived consequence of the war.

The European Union's statistics agency Monday said the combined gross domestic product of the eurozone's 21 members was 0.6% higher in the second quarter than in the three months through March, having stagnated in the first quarter.

That was an upward revision from the 0.4% figure previously published by Eurostat and largely reflected much stronger growth in Ireland than earlier recorded. On an annualized basis, the eurozone economy grew by 2.6%, outpacing the U.S., which expanded by 1.5%.
That left the eurozone as the only one of the world's major economies to record an acceleration during the period from April through June. The U.S., China, Japan and India all slowed.

There are indications that the eurozone economy has continued to expand at a robust pace. A survey of purchasing managers released last week found that business activity in August increased at the same pace as in July, which itself was an eight-month high.

"Momentum in the industrial economy has picked up nicely and the service sector has shaken off the initial weakness seen after energy prices surged at the start of the Middle East war," said Joe Hayes, an economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence.

A pickup in growth was not what most economists expected when they saw energy prices shoot higher as the U.S. and Israel launched their first attacks on Iran in late February. As an energy importer, the eurozone economy was expected to suffer as spending that was usually directed to goods and services largely made within the currency area instead swelled the coffers of  overseas oil and natural gas suppliers.

"These developments suggest that Europe is growing at, or even above, potential," economists at HSBC wrote in a note to clients. "That is remarkable, given the energy shock from the Middle East conflict."

In response to recent data, HSBC has raised its eurozone growth forecast for this year to 0.8% from the 0.3% it expected when the war started. That is not exactly stellar by international standards, but it is not far off the eurozone's recent average.
Instead of holding back on purchases of goods and services made in the eurozone as energy became more expensive, households appear to have drawn on their savings to keep spending.

Eurostat said consumer spending increased by 0.4% on the quarter, an acceleration from the 0.1% rate of growth recorded in the first three months of the year.  The big exception was motor fuels, purchases of which were 4.2% lower in June than a year earlier.
The other surprise has been a pickup in eurozone exports, which had been under pressure when the war began. Eurostat said exports were 3.4% higher than in the first quarter.

The good news on growth has implications for the European Central Bank, which meets Wednesday and Thursday and is expected to raise its key interest rate to 2.5% from 2.25%, having lifted borrowing costs in June for the first time since September 2023.

For policymakers, resilience reduces the risk that a rise in borrowing costs to contain a pickup in inflation will send the economy into a tailspin. It also makes it slightly more likely that the rise in energy costs for businesses will be fully passed on to the consumers, keeping inflation higher for longer.

However, it seems likely that support for eurozone growth will fade as the year advances. There are already some signs of fragility, with eurozone retail sales falling in July, as did German industrial production.
Home heating bills are likely to take a bigger bite from disposable incomes as temperatures drop, and households may become reluctant to dip further into their savings.
"If energy prices remain elevated, risks are that we will start to see a deterioration in private consumption towards the end of this year," economists at Morgan Stanley wrote in a note to clients.
The boost to exports may also prove short-lived, since it in part reflects disruptions to the supply of chemicals to Asian buyers from other sources since the start of the war.

Many economists and government officials see Europe facing a long-term challenge to its export-led growth model as a result of higher energy costs, increased tariffs, and fierce competition from China, with 2026 marking only a temporary reprieve.
"The external environment that sustained the eurozone's export-led model for decades has changed for good," wrote economists at ING Bank.
